runtimeContribution.transientBackoffMaxM.remediation: Raise this value in config/limits/runtimeContribution.yaml if the provider's Retry-After or recovery time is longer; DOCSFAB_RUNTIME_CONTRIBUTION_TRANSIENT_BACKOFF_MAX_MS may only lower it.
runtimeContribution.transientBackoffMaxM.rationale: Provisional, unmeasured. Longest single wait between retried attempts of one request, and the cap on a provider Retry-After value. Azure token rate limits are per-minute windows, so one minute covers a full window. A retry that would pass the cell deadline is not attempted and the cell stops with that response's code. The host override may only lower it.

runtimeContribution.adapterTextMaxBytes.remediation: A clipped text ends with a [truncated] line, and result-capture.json sets the matching truncated flag (resultText, pendingQuestion or stepSummaries). Read the full text in the cell's retained run record or with docsfab runs show against its exported state. If representative cells legitimately exceed the bound, raise runtimeContribution.adapterTextMaxBytes in config/limits/runtimeContribution.yaml through a reviewed change, recompute the stdout headroom in its rationale, and qualify a new campaign. No host setting changes this value.
runtimeContribution.adapterTextMaxBytes.rationale: UTF-8 bytes the DocsFab benchmark adapter keeps of each text it returns or retains - the original-scoring finalText and terminalReason, the amended capture's runs show text and pending question, and each step summary and error. It is a fixed capture bound, sealed with no override, because the adapter runs inside the live container, which receives no host limit settings; a host value would show in doctor but never reach a run. Bounded because the live child writes the whole adapter result as one JSON line to a stdout that run/live.mjs stops at 16 MiB. Four bounded texts travel on that line - finalText, terminalReason, resultText and the pending question; step summaries are cut here but written only to result-capture.json. Each is at most 524288 bytes plus a 12-byte newline-[truncated] marker, and JSON escaping writes at most six bytes for each kept byte, so the four take at most 4 x 524288 x 6 bytes (12 MiB) plus their escaped markers. The remaining 4 MiB must carry the run record, whose steps hold the uncut summaries and errors, plus the capture errors, provider report and events, and child diagnostics. This bound does not cut those, and no test measures the combined worst case. Measured basis, one round (gpt-6-sol, 2026-10-05 pilot, 30 cells) - the largest final text was 48960 bytes and the largest runs show text 10445 bytes, so the value leaves about ten times the largest measured text. It carries the former adapter literal (512 KiB, 2026-09-15) unchanged, so original-scoring bytes do not move.

bench.nightly.readbackDriftClauseMaxChar.remediation: Read the run record's executionReadback and each settled cell's evidence for every differing field; the public clause then gives each arm's count of fields instead of their names.
bench.nightly.readbackDriftClauseMaxChar.rationale: Longest public execution-readback-drift clause the nightly appends to run.statusReason after spend. Up to this length the clause names every differing field per arm; a longer one names each arm's count of differing fields and points to the run record, which keeps every field for every cell. A single drifted cell names a few fields of about 30 characters each, so 600 holds a typical difference whole and keeps a reason on the progress page readable. It shapes public text only, never a cell, a status or the comparison series.

bench.nightly.judgeQuoteMaxChars.remediation: Quote a shorter exact span from the supplied evidence. Changing this fixed J1 judge policy requires a new prompt and scoring-contract review, not a host override.
bench.nightly.judgeQuoteMaxChars.rationale: The owner-authored J1 judge prompt requires each exact evidence quote to be under 300 characters. This exclusive bound is reused by the rendered prompt and reply parser so they cannot drift. It controls citation evidence shape, not provider spending, request count, or model output tokens; a change creates a new judge prompt and comparison series.

bench.nightly.judgeMaxOutputTokens.remediation: Retain the unassessed judgment and its per-call diagnostics when the judge truncates; a lower override needs a reviewed reason and starts a new comparison series.
bench.nightly.judgeMaxOutputTokens.rationale: The checked-in aws/anthropic/bedrock-claude-sonnet-5 profile's maxOutputTokens. The selected panel's largest authored rubric has 22 criteria, each returned as structured JSON with an exact evidence quote under 300 characters and a reason. Pipeline 73185690 (2026-10-12) ran J1 at 16384 output tokens; one of its nine judge calls ended without a stop finish, most likely truncated. So the default is now the profile maximum, which leaves no smaller hidden response cap. The judge request also sends thinking disabled, as the judge profile declares (reasoning false) and the product does for this model and route, because the Hub's default thinking counts against this cap. In the seven nights that kept call diagnostics a first reply used a median of 1073 completion tokens per graded criterion against 250 in a repair reply that wrote the same grades again, and 10 of 110 first replies used more than half of the cap. The effective value is a public judge setting and a series limit, so changing it starts a new comparison series. A truncated reply is retried within bench.nightly.judgeRetries and never repaired. The separate shared USD reservations still bound all requests.

bench.nightly.judgeRepairTurns.remediation: Keep the cell unassessed with its per-call judge diagnostics, which list every validator problem of the last refused reply; review those problems before allowing more repair turns, which starts a new comparison series.
bench.nightly.judgeRepairTurns.rationale: Repair turns one judgment may take after a reply the validator refused (not JSON, a wrong packet binding, an invalid grade, an invalid evidence quote or a missing grade). Each turn quotes every validator problem back to the judge with its exact rule and criterion, with the packet, rubric and evidence unchanged, and its reply is validated by the same rules. Pipelines 73277557 to 73673854 (2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13) sent 115 cells to the judge, and 26 first replies were refused. The earlier single repair turn named only the first problem and fixed 21 of them. The other 5 failed again on a different criterion that the validator only reached after the first was fixed (four on one task, one on another), so the observed need is 2 turns and the bound is 2x that. A repair reply is short (median 3.4 thousand completion tokens against 7.8 thousand for a first reply), so the turns fit the 30 minute judge deadline. With bench.nightly.judgeRetries a judgment makes at most 1 + 3 + 4 = 8 calls. Through the real ledger a request of 1.3 MB, larger than any panel packet, fits all 8 calls that return replies (7.6 USD) or the 4 calls that fail without usage (9.2 USD) inside the 15.57 USD per-cell judge allowance and the cell's token budget, and a request above about 1.5 MB reaches that token budget first, where the refusal is recorded. A series limit.

bench.nightly.judgeRetries.remediation: Keep the cell unassessed with the cause of its last failed call in its note (an HTTP status or an error class) and in its per-call diagnostics; raise the count only for a measured reason, which starts a new comparison series.
bench.nightly.judgeRetries.rationale: Times one judgment re-sends an unchanged request after a failure that a fresh attempt can fix. These are a network error, a body that is not JSON, a response that did not finish (any finish reason other than stop, in practice length), a response with no content, and a reply that is still not JSON once its repair turns are spent. A transient provider status (HTTP 429, 502, 503 or 504) is retried first by the judge's own boundary under the declared runtimeContribution policy, as for the agent, so the judge retries one itself only through a boundary that carries no retries. Each retry waits bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffInitialMs, doubling up to bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffMaxMs. In pipelines 73277557 to 73673854 one of the 6 judgments of grove-gr1-ondelete-update-strategy ended without a stop finish (truncated at 32768 completion tokens), and 3 of the 50 judged cells of pipeline 73185690 ended unassessed as response-incomplete under the former 16384 token cap, so one retry clears most truncations and three leave well under one percent if truncations recur independently. The 183 judge requests of eight nights saw no transient provider status, so the transport retries are insurance for short blips. Without a Retry-After the waits are 2, 4 and 8 seconds, where the agent's eight retries cover about four minutes. A retry is a new request through the same budgeted judge boundary, so it reserves its own maximum, counts against the cell's judge allowance and shares its 30 minute deadline, and none starts when the backoff alone would pass that deadline. A failure no retry can fix (a request over the context bound, a refused reservation, a wrong model, an unknown cost) is never retried. With the repair turns a judgment makes at most 1 + 3 + 4 = 8 calls, which bench.nightly.judgeRepairTurns shows fit the allowance. A series limit.

bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffInitialMs.remediation: Raise this value in the catalog if the provider needs longer to recover between judge retries; the delay only paces retries and never starts a new comparison series.
bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffInitialMs.rationale: Wait before the first judge retry. Each later retry doubles it up to bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffMaxMs, and a numeric Retry-After from the provider replaces the doubling, still capped by the maximum. It is the same 2 second start the agent's transient retries use for the same provider. Provisional and unmeasured, because the 183 judge requests of eight nights saw no transient provider status. Timing only, so it is not part of the series.

bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffMaxMs.remediation: Raise this value in the catalog if the provider's Retry-After or recovery time is longer; the delay only paces retries and never starts a new comparison series.
bench.nightly.judgeRetryBackoffMaxMs.rationale: Longest single wait between judge retries, and the cap on a provider Retry-After. Provider token rate limits are per-minute windows, so one minute covers a full window, as for the agent's transient retries. With the default of three retries the doubling from 2 seconds waits 2, 4 and 8 seconds, so the cap only binds a long Retry-After. A rate-limit window longer than those waits is covered only by a provider Retry-After, or by the boundary's own retries, which the judge's limits now carry. A wait that would use the judgment's remaining deadline is not started. Provisional and unmeasured. Timing only, so it is not part of the series.

bench.nightly.judgeMinBytesPerToken.remediation: Keep the estimate at or below the fewest bytes per token that the judge's measured requests show. Setting 1 restores the old rule that counts every request byte as a token. A value above the measured minimum risks a provider refusal that is only seen after the send, and starts a new comparison series.
bench.nightly.judgeMinBytesPerToken.rationale: Fewest UTF-8 bytes one judge request token is assumed to span. It is used only to estimate a request's tokens against bench.nightly.judgeContextWindowTokens before the send. In pipelines 73277557 to 73673854 the provider's reported input tokens put 136 measured judge requests at 2.06 to 2.83 bytes per token (median 2.42), so 2 stays an upper bound on the tokens of every measured request. Counting every byte as a token (1) sat within 3 percent of the largest judged request (946558 bytes against a 967232 byte allowance). Every delivered gravitino-gv1 judgment of eight nights (7 of the 29 unassessed cells) failed before any provider request was reserved, and that task's blind packet carries its selected pages and code several times over, so it is the packet this estimate most plausibly refused. The cell's note now names the cause of such a failure. A request the estimate wrongly admits is refused by the provider and recorded with its status. A series limit.

bench.nightly.diagnosticStderrTailBytes.remediation: Read the retained tail in the private run record; raise it only after reviewing what the participant writes to stderr.
bench.nightly.diagnosticStderrTailBytes.rationale: When a released participant leaves no parseable result, the private run record keeps the last 4096 bytes of its container log, after credential-shape redaction, beside the exit code and OOM flag. Pipeline 73185690 lost the cause of a 0.75-second cell because only a digest of that log was kept. Four KiB holds a Node stack trace and the CLI's final error lines. It is diagnostic only, is never published, and never changes a cell.

bench.nightly.failedCellRecordMaxBytes.remediation: Read the retained copy in the failed cell's evidence in the arm checkpoint. An index over this bound keeps its newest rows from a row boundary, and the entry names the observed and the retained bytes. If representative failed cells legitimately exceed it, raise bench.nightly.failedCellRecordMaxBytes in config/limits/bench.yaml, up to its maximum. It only sizes retention and never changes a cell or the comparison series.
bench.nightly.failedCellRecordMaxBytes.rationale: Largest copy of a failed DocsFab cell's run index that the arm keeps in its private evidence. The eight measured nights of 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13 (pipelines 73185690 to 73673854) retained no run index at all, so the cause of their 21 provider-http-server DocsFab cells had to be rebuilt from the ledger. The run index holds one content-free row per run, step and attempt, with the provider's HTTP status, the failure class and the latency. The two eight-case matrices of 2026-09-23 together indexed to about 200 KiB, so a complete case is on the order of 10 KiB. A failed cell repeats a step up to seven times (one attempt and retry.maxTransportRetries retries), so its index is on the order of 100 KiB, and the value of 1 MiB is about ten times that, so only an extreme cell is cut. A cut keeps the newest rows, which hold the latest complete snapshot, from a row boundary, and says so in the evidence entry with this limit's refusal code, the observed bytes and the retained bytes. At most 20 cells fail in one arm, so the arm keeps at most 20 MiB. Provisional and unmeasured for failed nightly cells. The copy is never published, never judged and never changes a cell, so it is not part of the series.

bench.nightly.readerMaxArtifactBytes.remediation: Raise the nightly evaluator reader bound only after reviewing the verified writer's effective artifacts.maxObjectBytes setting and starting a new comparison series. Keep the entire sealed record and mark a reader-only size refusal as unassessed; never clip bytes.
bench.nightly.readerMaxArtifactBytes.rationale: The default 134217728 bytes equals the current verified DocsFab artifact writer's catalog default, so the evaluator adds no smaller hidden record cap. The maximum follows that writer catalog's supported 536870887-byte domain. This is a per-object reader bound for one sealed decision or rationale; a writer host override above the effective nightly value is a harness evidence fault, not a product quality failure. The effective value enters the public nightly conditions and changing it creates a new comparison series. The selected real-panel rationale records fit far below the default; the first manual qualification measures the current hosted journey.

bench.nightly.judgeContextWindowTokens.remediation: Retain the unassessed cell and full selected evidence. Review a new explicit source-file selector or model profile and start a new comparison series; never clip the prompt or omit a criterion.
bench.nightly.judgeContextWindowTokens.rationale: The checked-in aws/anthropic/bedrock-claude-sonnet-5 profile declares a 1000000-token context window and maxInputTokens. Before a judge send, the nightly estimates the request's tokens as its UTF-8 JSON bytes divided by bench.nightly.judgeMinBytesPerToken, rounded up, and adds the full declared output cap; values above this fixed profile capacity refuse with all selected evidence retained, and the refusal names this limit's code, the observed estimate and this value in the cell's note. This is model capacity, not a smaller sampling budget or a permission to truncate source files; a model profile change requires new qualification and series identity.

bench.nightly.agentContextWindowTokens.remediation: Retain the request and compare a newly documented model profile before changing this fixed capacity or comparison series; never clip task context.
bench.nightly.agentContextWindowTokens.rationale: The official GPT-6.1 Sol model page declares a 1050000-token context window. This checked-in model capacity is shared by DocsFab and both controls; the hosted alias has not been tested at that ceiling. Provider refusal is a coded cell outcome, never a silent truncation.

bench.nightly.agentMaxInputTokens.remediation: Retain the full task and review a separately documented input ceiling before introducing any smaller limit or clipping source material.
bench.nightly.agentMaxInputTokens.rationale: The official GPT-6.1 Sol model page publishes a 1050000-token context window but no independent max-input figure. The profile sets maxInputTokens equal to that context, deliberately adding no smaller benchmark input cap. The nightly attests the profile with the owner-approved model page, so DocsFab and both controls admit each request against this window and the context reserve before sending it; an unattested profile would leave admission to the provider.

bench.nightly.agentMaxOutputTokens.remediation: Retain the stopped or incomplete cell and review the official model capacity before changing the profile; never mark a truncated answer complete.
bench.nightly.agentMaxOutputTokens.rationale: The official GPT-6.1 Sol model page declares 128000 max output tokens. The hosted alias has been verified for small tool calls, not a 128000-token reply. DocsFab and both controls use this one effective output ceiling and the same complete-trial USD reservation ledger.

bench.nightly.agentContextReserveTokens.remediation: Review context admission for all three arms and begin a new comparison series before changing the fixed reserve; do not silently reduce it.
bench.nightly.agentContextReserveTokens.rationale: The owner accepted 4096 reserved context tokens for this GPT-6.1 Sol benchmark profile. Because the nightly attests the profile, DocsFab and both controls hold it back from the input window when they admit a request, as one shared framing and headroom policy for every arm. It is not a separate task sampling budget or a claim about a hosted hard limit.

bench.nightly.upstreamResponseMaxBytes.remediation: Retain the cell and its gateway diagnostic. Measure the provider's bytes per streamed output token on retained responses, raise this bound together with bench.nightly.gatewayMemoryBytes, and start a new comparison series; never truncate a response.
bench.nightly.upstreamResponseMaxBytes.rationale: Largest single provider response the nightly gateway reads, for an agent stream or a judge reply, sized from bench.nightly.agentMaxOutputTokens. The gateway buffers a whole response before it returns anything, and a streamed chat completion carries roughly one chunk of 200 to 300 bytes per visible output token, so 128000 tokens need about 34 MB. 64 MiB is about twice that; hidden reasoning tokens send no chunks. The previous 8 MiB literal held about 31000 streamed tokens, below the declared output. A response above it ends the cell's provider boundary with a coded refusal naming the observed and allowed bytes. Unmeasured on the Hub; it is a series limit.

bench.nightly.upstreamMaxContentCodings.remediation: Retain the cell and its gateway diagnostic and ask the provider why one response stacks this many content codings; never decode a longer chain.
bench.nightly.upstreamMaxContentCodings.rationale: Most content codings the nightly gateway's Hub transport undoes for one response, the same five Node's fetch (undici 7.24) allows. Each coding is one more decoder over the whole body, so a longer chain only multiplies decode work. A real Hub reply carries at most one. A longer chain ends the call with a coded refusal naming the count; nothing is decoded. It is a series limit only because the transport decides whether a reply is read.

bench.nightly.gatewayMemoryBytes.remediation: Raise DOCSFAB_BENCH_NIGHTLY_GATEWAY_MEMORY_BYTES for this host, up to the catalog max, when the gateway sidecar is killed for memory; it can never go below the default, which a response at bench.nightly.upstreamResponseMaxBytes needs.
bench.nightly.gatewayMemoryBytes.rationale: Memory limit of the nightly gateway sidecar container. Reading one response, the sidecar holds several copies of it while it screens, meters, parses and returns it. At bench.nightly.upstreamResponseMaxBytes, a 64 MiB streamed response measured about 520 MiB above the process baseline in the fixture sidecar, and one of two-byte UTF-8 text 684 to 746 MiB, before TLS and HTTP buffers (2026-10-14). 2 GiB leaves more than twice the largest measured need, and a nightly host has about 23 GB. Requests are one at a time per cell. The shared benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes default of 256 MiB held the former 8 MiB bound at about half its memory. It is a series limit because a sidecar killed for memory ends the arm.

bench.nightly.cellTimeoutMs.remediation: Preserve the stopped cell and remaining work. Qualify a changed complete-cell deadline across all three arms and start a new comparison series before raising it.
bench.nightly.cellTimeoutMs.rationale: The nightly retained its 1800000 ms declared complete-cell deadline as a common benchmark fairness policy while moving from the previous GPT-6 Sol composition path to the owner-selected GPT-6.1 Sol profile path. It covers participant, helpers, retries, and judging with no smaller layer cap; it is not a provider model-capacity claim or a historical parity claim. Manual qualification must measure whether the supported 20-cell arm fits within the CI job.

bench.nightly.estimatedMicroUsdPerMillio.remediation: Use an integer microUSD-per-million-total-tokens override at or above the owner-accepted Oct 6–8 blended estimator. A billed rate or lower estimator needs a separately reviewed policy update; this field is not spending authority.
bench.nightly.estimatedMicroUsdPerMillio.rationale: The owner accepted the Oct 6–8 benchmark spend watcher's blended ESTIMATED 1.73 USD per million total tokens for the new GPT-6.1 Sol series, with basis labelled estimate rather than billed. The integer microUSD representation preserves that estimator exactly. The minimum is raise-only; the maximum is JavaScript safe-integer representation, not a provider price, purchase approval, or budget. The distinct 8 USD complete-trial reservation and the scheduled-run cap remain authoritative, and overflow refuses before a send.

bench.nightly.perTrialMaxUsd.remediation: Retain the trial's accounting and unfinished work, inspect participant, helper, and retry requests, then raise DOCSFAB_BENCH_NIGHTLY_PER_TRIAL_MAX_USD only with owner approval if representative work needs more headroom. A scheduled run's per-arm share of the run cap still applies separately.
bench.nightly.perTrialMaxUsd.rationale: The owner set an 8 USD default on 2026-10-08 for one complete task-arm trial's participant requests, helpers, and retries. Judging is not in it. Each admitted cell gets its own judge allowance, the judge's context window times its attempts at the estimated rate (about 15.57 USD per cell at the defaults), which the ledger caps separately. Historical selected DocsFab cells reached 5.147 USD, so the default allows that measured journey with roughly 55 percent headroom. The 9000 USD override-domain maximum prevents configuring one trial above the dedicated credential's entire monthly provider cap; it does not convert that cap into trial funding or authorize raising the default. The separate scheduled-run cap applies only to a scheduled run, split into declared shares across its independent arms.

bench.nightly.scheduledRunSpendCapUsd.remediation: Keep the arm's ledger, settled cells and unstarted slots, then review measured provider spend. Raise DOCSFAB_BENCH_NIGHTLY_SCHEDULED_RUN_SPEND_CAP_USD for this host, up to the monthly provider key cap, only after the owner approves more spend per scheduled run. A manual web run has no run-level cap.
bench.nightly.scheduledRunSpendCapUsd.rationale: The owner set 100 USD for the whole 20-task, three-arm nightly run on 2026-10-08, applied it to scheduled runs only on 2026-10-12, and raised it to 130 USD the same day ("Fine, raise the budget to $130", recorded in owner-cost-approval.json). A manual web run has no run-level cap. The three arms run as independent jobs with job-local ledgers and no shared ledger, so each arm of a scheduled run enforces its own declared share; the three shares sum to this cap, which keeps the run at or below it whatever the other arms spend. An arm that reaches its share stops admitting cells and labels the rest; it never stops another arm. An arm refuses to start when its overridden shares sum above this cap. Pipeline 73185690 measured about 2.9 USD per executed docsfab-do cell and about 1.6 USD per skills-agent cell, which projects about 58 and 32 USD for full arms. The 8 USD per-trial cap applies to every run, and the dedicated credential's 9000 USD monthly provider cap is the backstop; the 9000 USD override-domain maximum keeps one run below that monthly cap and does not authorize spending it.

bench.nightly.docsfabDoSpendShareUsd.remediation: Keep the docsfab-do arm's settled cells and its labelled unstarted slots, then rebalance the three arm shares of the scheduled-run cap from measured per-arm cost. The three shares must not sum above bench.nightly.scheduledRunSpendCapUsd; raise the cap itself only with owner approval.
bench.nightly.docsfabDoSpendShareUsd.rationale: The docsfab-do arm's share of the 130 USD scheduled-run cap. Arms run as independent jobs with job-local ledgers. A scheduled arm starts a cell while any headroom remains under its own share, and every request reserves its maximum before it is sent and is refused if it would cross the share, so the three shares, which sum to the cap, keep the run at or below it. 70 USD is about 20 percent above the projected full-arm cost of about 58 USD; pipeline 73185690 (2026-10-12) measured about 2.9 USD per executed docsfab-do cell. A manual web run has no share and no run-level cap.

bench.nightly.skillsAgentSpendShareUsd.remediation: Keep the skills-agent arm's settled cells and its labelled unstarted slots, then rebalance the three arm shares of the scheduled-run cap from measured per-arm cost. The three shares must not sum above bench.nightly.scheduledRunSpendCapUsd; raise the cap itself only with owner approval.
bench.nightly.skillsAgentSpendShareUsd.rationale: The skills-agent arm's share of the 130 USD scheduled-run cap. Arms run as independent jobs with job-local ledgers. A scheduled arm starts a cell while any headroom remains under its own share, and every request reserves its maximum before it is sent and is refused if it would cross the share, so the three shares, which sum to the cap, keep the run at or below it. 38 USD is about 20 percent above the projected full-arm cost of about 32 USD; pipeline 73185690 measured about 1.6 USD per skills-agent cell over its first three cells. A manual web run has no share and no run-level cap.

bench.nightly.basicAgentSpendShareUsd.remediation: Keep the basic-agent arm's settled cells and its labelled unstarted slots, then rebalance the three arm shares of the scheduled-run cap from measured per-arm cost. The three shares must not sum above bench.nightly.scheduledRunSpendCapUsd; raise the cap itself only with owner approval.
bench.nightly.basicAgentSpendShareUsd.rationale: The basic-agent arm's share of the 130 USD scheduled-run cap. Arms run as independent jobs with job-local ledgers. A scheduled arm starts a cell while any headroom remains under its own share, and every request reserves its maximum before it is sent and is refused if it would cross the share, so the three shares, which sum to the cap, keep the run at or below it. 22 USD is the rest of the cap; the basic-agent arm was not yet measured and is presumed the cheapest, and its share will be refined from measured nights. A manual web run has no share and no run-level cap.

benchmarks.manifest.maxBytes.remediation: Split the task or move long material out of the manifest; a manifest holds pointers and our own authored criteria, never upstream bytes. If an authored task legitimately needs more, raise benchmarks.manifest.maxBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.manifest.maxBytes.rationale: Largest task manifest file validate reads before parsing it. A manifest holds a trigger, pointers, and authored criteria; a task with 40 criteria of a few hundred characters each is under 32 KiB. 256 KiB leaves room for long triggers and usage scenarios while keeping a pasted upstream file or a binary out of the parser. Unmeasured planning value; the first dev-tier corpus is the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.manifest.maxTextChars.remediation: Shorten the named field; a trigger, rubric, or evidence note is authored prose, not a copy of upstream material. If an authored field legitimately needs more, raise benchmarks.manifest.maxTextChars in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.manifest.maxTextChars.rationale: Longest single string field in a task manifest (trigger, rubric, condition, evidence, usage prompt). A long issue-style trigger is a few thousand characters; 16384 allows about four times that while refusing a pasted document. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.manifest.maxVerbatimChars.remediation: Paraphrase the quoted span in your own words, or quote only the identifier, flag, config key, or path the criterion needs. If a criterion legitimately needs a longer literal, raise benchmarks.manifest.maxVerbatimChars in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml and record why in the review.
benchmarks.manifest.maxVerbatimChars.rationale: Longest quoted span (double quotes, curly quotes, a code span, or a fenced block) allowed in a trigger, criterion rubric or condition, or expected evidence, and the longest required or forbidden text a deterministic check may match. It bounds verbatim upstream quotation in our authored criteria (the plan section on real inputs). Flag names, config keys, file paths, and identifiers are well under 120 characters; a quoted upstream paragraph is not. Unmeasured planning value; writer review of the first dev tasks is the basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.corpus.maxManifestsPerTier.remediation: Check the tier directory for stray or generated files. If the corpus legitimately grew past it, raise benchmarks.corpus.maxManifestsPerTier in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.corpus.maxManifestsPerTier.rationale: Most entries validate reads from one corpus tier directory before reading any of them. The plan grows the dev tier toward 300 tasks and keeps held-out tasks outside this repository, so 1000 is more than three times the planned tier size.

benchmarks.run.maxFileBytes.remediation: Inspect the named file; a run result that carries a whole repository or a log is a harness defect, not a patch. If a representative documentation patch legitimately exceeds it, raise benchmarks.run.maxFileBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.run.maxFileBytes.rationale: Largest run-config, run-result, judgment, retained patch, or report file score, rescore, and report read before parsing, and the largest prepared record (attestation, attribution, masking map) verify-prepared reads. A documentation patch across a few dozen pages is under 1 MiB; 16 MiB keeps a pasted repository or log out of the parser. Unmeasured planning value; the first live run is the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.run.maxTrials.remediation: Lower the run's repeats or split the run by tier. If a campaign legitimately needs more trials in one report, raise benchmarks.run.maxTrials in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.run.maxTrials.rationale: Most trials (tasks times arms times repeats) one run directory may declare, and most run-result or judgment files score reads from it. The planned campaign is 300 tasks, three arms, and a handful of repeats, about 4500 trials; 10000 leaves room for a larger repeat count without reading an unbounded directory.

benchmarks.run.maxPhysicalSendsPerTrial.remediation: Inspect the trial's provider loop and retry policy; if a supported workflow legitimately needs more sends, raise this catalog entry after measuring one representative run.
benchmarks.run.maxPhysicalSendsPerTrial.rationale: Maximum physically dispatched model requests in one arm trial, including admission, workflow retries, and agent turns. The existing composition turn ceiling is 512 for one step; 4096 admits several steps plus retries and leaves substantial room for a three-arm representative run. Unmeasured planning value pending protected execution.

benchmarks.run.armWallTimeoutMs.remediation: Inspect the stopped arm and provider latency; raise this catalog entry only if a representative supported task needs more execution time.
benchmarks.run.armWallTimeoutMs.rationale: Wall duration from one arm container start to exit, including provider backoff. A composition step can run for up to one hour, so four hours admits a multi-step workflow without silently shortening its own timer. This is an outer safety bound, not a model or token budget. Unmeasured planning value pending protected execution.

benchmarks.usage.verifierTimeoutMs.remediation: Inspect the offline verifier output and the host load. If the accepted executable verifier legitimately needs longer, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_USAGE_VERIFIER_TIMEOUT_MS for this host within the catalog range.
benchmarks.usage.verifierTimeoutMs.rationale: Wall deadline for one offline usage fixture verifier process, including its Python interpreter and the accepted CPU task command. The committed verifier bounds its inner command at 120 seconds; 180 seconds gives interpreter startup and checks time around it without turning a stalled subprocess into an unbounded benchmark run. Early seven-trial scripted campaigns finished in 3 to 6 seconds locally and in the Node 24 Bookworm image; a later contended local run took 11 seconds. One verifier is far below 180 seconds in these observations, but the default is provisional pending representative loaded-runner evidence. This is host execution capacity, not a correctness score; the effective value is recorded with each trial identity.

benchmarks.run.exportMaxEntries.remediation: Inspect the arm's bounded state and artifact output; raise this entry only for a measured supported workflow with more retained files.
benchmarks.run.exportMaxEntries.rationale: Maximum files and directories under one arm-only export root before host import. Product run records and editorial artifacts occupy far fewer entries in a normal task; this stops an unbounded participant output tree. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.run.exportMaxBytes.remediation: Inspect the arm's state artifact sizes; retain only outcome and usage evidence, or raise this entry for a measured supported workflow.
benchmarks.run.exportMaxBytes.rationale: Maximum aggregate bytes under one arm-only export root before import. Individual result and record files also obey the shared run file bound; 64 MiB allows several product records while rejecting a repository or provider transcript. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.relayRequestMaxBytes.remediation: Inspect the model request size and the installed composition's context limits; raise only for a representative supported request that exceeds this bound.
benchmarks.sandbox.relayRequestMaxBytes.rationale: Maximum single model request body transferred from an arm through the credential-free relay to the job custodian. The installed model accepts a large context and several megabytes of text; 16 MiB is above its ordinary serialized request while preventing an unbounded in-memory relay body. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.relayResponseMaxBytes.remediation: Inspect the provider's response or event stream; raise only if the installed composition admits a larger supported response.
benchmarks.sandbox.relayResponseMaxBytes.rationale: Maximum single provider response body held and returned by the job custodian. The composition's response ceiling is 4 MiB, so 8 MiB admits its complete serialized stream with transport framing while bounding both memory and control traffic. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.relayReadyTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the relay container's bounded startup status and the dind published-port mapping; raise this host override only for measured slow starts.
benchmarks.sandbox.relayReadyTimeoutMs.rationale: Maximum wait after a validated relay starts for the job-side outbound mTLS control channel to answer readiness. Node listener startup is normally seconds; 30 seconds allows a loaded runner without permitting an absent route to hold the trial indefinitely. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.relayPendingMaxReques.remediation: Inspect the arm's concurrent model requests; raise this entry only after showing the larger queue fits benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes.
benchmarks.sandbox.relayPendingMaxReques.rationale: Most in-flight arm model requests retained by the relay. At the 16 MiB request-body ceiling, four raw bodies and their base64 control copies use about 150 MiB, leaving headroom in the gateway's 256 MiB service memory. A normal Pi agent sends one request at a time. Expired and closed requests leave the queue immediately.

benchmarks.prepare.fetchTimeoutMs.remediation: Check the network path to the source host, or prepare from a local mirror with --source-mirror. If the host's link is legitimately slower, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_PREPARE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.prepare.fetchTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest wall-clock time DocsFab Bench prepare lets one git command run. The shallow fetch of a single pinned commit is the longest such command; the local commands (init, ls-tree, the blob batch, add, commit) on the same tree finish well inside it. Ten minutes covers a depth-1 fetch of a tree at the tree-bytes bound over a slow link. The host override exists because network latency is a host property, not task semantics. Unmeasured planning value; the first three smoke prepares are the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.prepare.maxTreeBytes.remediation: Pick a source whose pinned tree is smaller, or confirm the repository really needs this many bytes of blobs. If representative documentation repositories legitimately exceed it, raise benchmarks.prepare.maxTreeBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.prepare.maxTreeBytes.rationale: Largest sum of blob sizes in one pinned source tree, read from the tree listing before any blob is written. Documentation repositories with images run to a few hundred MiB; 1 GiB leaves room for one with large assets while keeping a monorepo or a dataset out of the output directory. Unmeasured planning value; the three smoke prepares and the largest mined candidate are the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.prepare.maxFiles.remediation: Pick a source with a smaller pinned tree, or confirm the repository really holds this many entries. If representative documentation repositories legitimately exceed it, raise benchmarks.prepare.maxFiles in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.prepare.maxFiles.rationale: Most entries in one pinned source tree, counting files, symlinks, submodule links, and every directory that holds them. Prepare counts them from the tree listing before any blob is written, and the seal walk of prepare and verify-prepared counts the same population on disk, so a tree that passes the listing never refuses at the seal. Large documentation sites hold tens of thousands of files in a few thousand directories; 100000 leaves room for one with many generated reference pages. Unmeasured planning value; the three smoke prepares are the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.prepare.maxFileBytes.remediation: Inspect the named file; a documentation source rarely carries a single blob this large. If a representative source legitimately does, raise benchmarks.prepare.maxFileBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.prepare.maxFileBytes.rationale: Largest single blob in a pinned source tree, read from the tree listing before any blob is written, and the largest file verify-prepared hashes. Large images and PDFs in documentation stay under tens of MiB; 100 MiB keeps a committed archive or dataset out. It stays under benchmarks.prepare.maxTreeBytes so the per-file bound fires first for a single large blob. Unmeasured planning value; the three smoke prepares are the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.prepare.maxGitOutputBytes.remediation: A git command printed far more than its listing or status needs; inspect the source tree for an unusual entry count or path length. If a representative source legitimately needs more, raise benchmarks.prepare.maxGitOutputBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.prepare.maxGitOutputBytes.rationale: Most bytes DocsFab Bench prepare and verify-prepared capture from stdout or stderr of one git command other than the blob batch. The only blob read through it is the license file, a few KiB; every other blob goes to a scratch file bounded by benchmarks.prepare.maxTreeBytes and benchmarks.prepare.maxFileBytes. The largest capture is the recursive tree listing, about 60 bytes plus the path per entry, so 64 MiB covers benchmarks.prepare.maxFiles entries with paths averaging over 500 bytes, and the combined defaults never refuse a listing that passes the entry-count bound.

benchmarks.sandbox.daemonReadyTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the dind service log in the job for a start-up error (certificate generation, storage driver, or privileged mode). If the runner is legitimately slower to start the service, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_DAEMON_READY_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.daemonReadyTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest time a DocsFab Bench job waits for the docker:dind service to answer an authenticated GET /_ping before it refuses with bench-sandbox-dind-missing. The service generates a CA, a server and a client key pair, then starts the daemon; on a shared runner that takes seconds, and two minutes covers a slow image pull of the service plus key generation. Only connection failures are retried inside this window; a TLS, API or lost-connection failure refuses at once. The host override exists because service start time is a runner property. Planning value; the milestone-1 job prints each channel's time to ready (its ok-after line, in milliseconds), which is the measured basis to revisit it.

benchmarks.sandbox.daemonPollIntervalMs.remediation: This is the pause between readiness attempts, not a bound an observed value can exceed; change it in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml only if the readiness wait polls too often or too rarely.
benchmarks.sandbox.daemonPollIntervalMs.rationale: Pause between two readiness attempts against the docker:dind service inside benchmarks.sandbox.daemonReadyTimeoutMs. One second keeps the wait within a second of the daemon becoming ready without flooding a service that is still generating keys; the default wait allows about 120 attempts.

benchmarks.sandbox.apiRequestTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the dind service log for a daemon that stopped answering. If the runner's daemon is legitimately slower, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_API_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.apiRequestTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest wall-clock time one Docker Engine API request from a DocsFab Bench job may take, from connect to the last response byte, other than an image pull or a container wait, which have their own bounds. Ping, version, info, create, start, logs, and remove answer in milliseconds on a healthy daemon, and the upstream seam probe applies the same deadline to its one TLS handshake inside its container; 30 seconds absorbs a loaded shared runner without letting a hung daemon hold the job. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.imagePullTimeoutMs.remediation: Check the runner's path to the image registry and the registry's rate limit for anonymous pulls. If the link is legitimately slower, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_IMAGE_PULL_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.imagePullTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest time one digest-pinned sandbox image pull inside the dind service may take. The dind daemon starts empty in every job, so each job pulls the sandbox image fresh; the Node bookworm image is about 400 MiB compressed, and ten minutes covers it over a slow shared link. The host override exists because registry latency is a host property. Measured basis, the milestone-1 job pulled the digest-pinned image in 8273 ms and 8982 ms on the shared Docker runners (two runs); ten minutes keeps a cold registry path and anonymous rate-limit back-off inside the bound.

benchmarks.sandbox.seamProbeTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the probe's recorded output for the step that hung (a bind-mount read or an upstream TLS handshake). If the runner is legitimately slower, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_SEAM_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.seamProbeTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest time one milestone seam-probe container may run, from start to exit. A bind-mount read and one TLS handshake finish in seconds; a minute covers container start on a loaded runner and a slow upstream handshake. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.apiResponseMaxBytes.remediation: Inspect the request that produced the response; a ping, version, create, or probe log does not legitimately reach this size. If a representative response does, raise benchmarks.sandbox.apiResponseMaxBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.sandbox.apiResponseMaxBytes.rationale: Most bytes a DocsFab Bench job reads from one Docker Engine API response body, one line of an image-pull progress stream, or one probe container's log. Version and info documents are a few KiB and a pull progress line is under 1 KiB; 1 MiB keeps a runaway log or a hostile response out of memory with a wide margin.

benchmarks.sandbox.workloadPidsLimit.remediation: Read the container's create-time inspect in the dind proof report. A PidsLimit of 0, -1 or null means unlimited and is never admitted. If a representative arm, judge, prepare or verifier run legitimately needs more processes, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_WORKLOAD_PIDS_LIMIT for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.workloadPidsLimit.rationale: Process-count limit (HostConfig.PidsLimit) of each workload-family sandbox container (arm, judge, prepare, verifier), one value per container. An agent arm runs Node, git and the product's own subprocesses; 1024 leaves room for a parallel install or test run while a fork bomb stops at the cgroup instead of exhausting the shared dind host. Per family, not per class, because no measurement yet separates an arm from a verifier. The catalog min of 1 is the daemon's own floor. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.workloadMemoryBytes.remediation: Read the container's create-time inspect and the printed MemTotal in the dind proof job log. Memory 0 means unlimited and is never admitted. If a representative workload legitimately needs more and the runner has the room, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_WORKLOAD_MEMORY_BYTES for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.workloadMemoryBytes.rationale: Memory limit (HostConfig.Memory, with MemorySwap equal to it where the daemon supports swap limits) of each workload-family sandbox container, one value per container; tmpfs pages count against it. 2 GiB holds a Node agent process, git and an npm install. The arm runs together with the gateway and the proxy, so the dind proof refuses before the first create when this plus both benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes exceed the daemon's MemTotal; MemTotal is the runner host's total, shared with the job container, the dind daemon and other concurrent jobs, so the 2.5 GiB sum must leave most of it free. The catalog min of 6 MiB is the daemon's own floor. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.workloadNanoCpus.remediation: Read the container's create-time inspect and the printed NCPU in the dind proof job log. NanoCpus 0 means unlimited and is never admitted. If the runner has fewer CPUs than this, lower DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_WORKLOAD_NANO_CPUS for this host; if a representative workload legitimately needs more, raise it, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.workloadNanoCpus.rationale: CPU limit (HostConfig.NanoCpus, in billionths of a CPU) of each workload-family sandbox container, one value per container. Two CPUs let an agent run a build or test step without starving the other jobs on a shared runner. The daemon refuses a value above its NCPU at create, so the dind proof checks it against GET /info before the first create. The catalog min of 10000000 (0.01 CPU) is the daemon's own floor. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.workloadTmpfsBytes.remediation: Read the tmpfs options in the container's create-time inspect. A tmpfs without a size defaults to half the host's memory and is never admitted. If a representative workload legitimately writes more scratch data, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_WORKLOAD_TMPFS_BYTES for this host, up to the catalog max, and keep it below benchmarks.sandbox.workloadMemoryBytes.
benchmarks.sandbox.workloadTmpfsBytes.rationale: Size of each tmpfs mount (the writable /tmp and, for an arm, the home directory that holds agent state outside the workspace) in a workload-family sandbox container. Per mount, not per class; tmpfs pages also count against the container's memory limit, which caps the sum. 512 MiB holds an npm cache and agent state for one trial. The catalog min of 1 MiB keeps a tmpfs usable. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.servicePidsLimit.remediation: Read the container's create-time inspect in the dind proof report. A PidsLimit of 0, -1 or null means unlimited and is never admitted. If the gateway or the proxy legitimately needs more processes, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_SERVICE_PIDS_LIMIT for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.servicePidsLimit.rationale: Process-count limit of each service-family container (the model gateway and the allowlist proxy), one value per container. Each is one Node process with a few worker threads; 256 is generous for that and still stops a runaway. The catalog min of 1 is the daemon's own floor. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes.remediation: Read the container's create-time inspect and the printed MemTotal in the dind proof job log. Memory 0 means unlimited and is never admitted. If the gateway or the proxy legitimately needs more, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_SERVICE_MEMORY_BYTES for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes.rationale: Memory limit of each service-family container (gateway, proxy), one value per container. A forwarding Node process stays well under 256 MiB. Both count, with the arm's benchmarks.sandbox.workloadMemoryBytes, in the pre-create MemTotal check. The catalog min of 6 MiB is the daemon's own floor. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.serviceNanoCpus.remediation: Read the container's create-time inspect and the printed NCPU in the dind proof job log. NanoCpus 0 means unlimited and is never admitted. If the gateway or the proxy legitimately needs more CPU, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_SERVICE_NANO_CPUS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.serviceNanoCpus.rationale: CPU limit of each service-family container (gateway, proxy), one value per container. Half a CPU forwards one trial's model and registry traffic. The dind proof checks it against the daemon's NCPU before the first create. The catalog min of 10000000 (0.01 CPU) is the daemon's own floor. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.serviceTmpfsBytes.remediation: Read the tmpfs options in the container's create-time inspect. A tmpfs without a size defaults to half the host's memory and is never admitted. If the gateway or the proxy legitimately writes more scratch data, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_SERVICE_TMPFS_BYTES for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.serviceTmpfsBytes.rationale: Size of each tmpfs mount (the writable /tmp) in a service-family container. Per mount, not per class; it also counts against the container's memory limit. The gateway and the proxy keep no state, so 64 MiB is scratch room only. The catalog min of 1 MiB keeps a tmpfs usable. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyConnectTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the proxy log line for the host; a registry that resolves and accepts a TCP connection does so in well under a second. If the runner's resolver or route to an allowlisted host is legitimately slower, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_PROXY_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyConnectTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest time the DocsFab Bench egress proxy spends on one CONNECT from the end of its request head to an open upstream socket, name resolution and the TCP dial together, before it answers 504. One timer spans both, so a resolver that never answers cannot hold a tunnel slot past it. The glibc resolver's own default is a 5-second timeout with two attempts, so 15 seconds covers one slow resolution plus a dial on a loaded runner, and stays well inside benchmarks.sandbox.seamProbeTimeoutMs so a probe that goes through the proxy reports the proxy's code, not its own timeout. The host override exists because resolver and route latency are runner properties. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyIdleTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the proxy log line for the host; a tunnel that moves no byte in either direction for this long is stalled. If a representative fetch legitimately pauses longer (a large git pack computed server side), raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_PROXY_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyIdleTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest time one egress proxy connection may go without a byte, read or written, before the proxy closes it; it also bounds reading a client's request head, so a client that opens a connection and sends nothing frees its slot. A registry download or a git fetch streams progress continuously, and two minutes covers a server-side pause such as pack generation. The host override exists because upstream latency is a runner property. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyMaxTunnels.remediation: Read the proxy log for the hosts that held the slots; a prepare step that opens this many connections at once is a runaway or a client without a socket limit. If a representative install legitimately needs more, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_PROXY_MAX_TUNNELS for this host, up to the catalog max, and keep the tunnels' buffers inside benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyMaxTunnels.rationale: Most client connections the egress proxy holds at once, counted from accept to the close of both sockets, so a connection still sending its request head holds a slot too; the next one is answered 503. A package manager opens at most a few dozen sockets per registry. Each tunnel buffers at most two sockets at Node's default stream highWaterMark in each direction (64 KiB on Node 24), so 64 tunnels hold 16 MiB, well inside the proxy's 256 MiB benchmarks.sandbox.serviceMemoryBytes. Kernel socket buffers are not counted here. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxEntr.remediation: List only the registry and source hosts the prepare step contacts; each entry is an exact host name, so a long list is usually a list of mirrors or a pasted file. If a representative task legitimately needs more hosts, raise benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxEntries in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxEntr.rationale: Most host names the egress proxy's allowlist may hold; a longer list refuses at load and the proxy does not start. A prepare step reaches a package registry, its download host and a source host or two, so 64 exact names leave wide room while a list that has grown into a mirror directory is caught. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxByte.remediation: List only exact host names in the allowlist JSON array, with no comments or other fields. If a representative allowlist legitimately needs more bytes, raise benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxByte.rationale: Most bytes of the egress proxy's allowlist, a JSON array of host names, checked before it is parsed; a larger one refuses at load. benchmarks.sandbox.proxyAllowlistMaxEntries names of up to 253 characters, quoted and comma-separated, fit in 16 KiB. The allowlist reaches the proxy as one argument of its command, and Linux caps one argument at 131072 bytes, so the catalog max stays at half of that. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyRequestMaxBytes.remediation: Read the proxy log line for the byte count; a CONNECT request head is one short line and a few headers, so a larger one is a client sending a body or junk before the tunnel opens. If a representative client legitimately sends more headers, raise benchmarks.sandbox.proxyRequestMaxBytes in config/limits/benchmarks.yaml.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyRequestMaxBytes.rationale: Most bytes of one CONNECT request head the egress proxy reads, the request line and every header up to and including the blank line that ends them; a longer head is answered 431 and closed. A CONNECT line for a 253-character host is under 300 bytes, and npm, git and curl add a handful of short headers, so 8 KiB leaves wide room, below Node's own 16 KiB default for HTTP headers. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.negativeProbeMaxAddre.remediation: Read the smoke job's denied-range lines for the networks and dind addresses it derived; a fresh dind daemon reports its default bridge and the run's own three networks, so a longer list means another network outlived an earlier run or the daemon was given extra networks. Remove the stray networks; if a representative daemon legitimately reports more, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_NEGATIVE_PROBE_MAX_ADDRESSES for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.negativeProbeMaxAddre.rationale: Most entries of the one address list the sandbox start path derives at launch, which the egress proxy takes as its denied ranges and the negative dind probe takes as its targets. It counts list entries, not probes. The list holds one entry per IPAM subnet of every network GET /networks reports, IPv4 and IPv6 apart, plus one per resolved address of each dind service alias. A longer list refuses, never truncates. A fresh dind daemon holds the default bridge and the run's gateway, proxy and egress networks, four subnets or eight when dual-stack, and the job sees two dind services; 16 covers that with room for a dual-stack daemon. Unmeasured planning value.

benchmarks.sandbox.proxyListenTimeoutMs.remediation: Read the proxy container's log and its state in the smoke report; a proxy that has neither listened nor exited this long after start is stuck in node start-up or in the daemon. If the runner is legitimately slower, raise DOCSFAB_BENCHMARKS_SANDBOX_PROXY_LISTEN_TIMEOUT_MS for this host, up to the catalog max.
benchmarks.sandbox.proxyListenTimeoutMs.rationale: Longest time the job waits, from the egress proxy container's start, for the proxy's listening record in its log, polling every benchmarks.sandbox.daemonPollIntervalMs. A proxy that exits first is reported by its own refusal code at once, not after this wait. Node starts and the proxy checks its inputs in well under a second; half a minute covers container start on a loaded runner. Unmeasured planning value.

nightly.panelTasks.remediation: Restore the owner-approved daily-v1 panel of 20 tasks; a different panel needs a new recorded selection and comparability key.
nightly.panelTasks.rationale: The owner confirmed 20 admitted real-world tasks, 13 update and 7 no-change, for the frozen daily-v1 panel on 2026-10-08. A partial panel is reported through cells and run status, never silently treated as a smaller benchmark.

nightly.cellParallelism.remediation: Keep the source stub's one-at-a-time execution, or qualify a new runner and shared-ledger design before raising this bound.
nightly.cellParallelism.rationale: The Phase 0 source-stub harness executes its 60 synthetic cells sequentially and has no qualified parallel shared-ledger path. One active cell is the supported journey until the live arm shards are implemented and measured.

nightly.ciJobTimeoutMs.remediation: Keep the paid 20-cell arm on a dedicated runner with a verified maximum timeout of at least 480 minutes; retain a partial checkpoint when time admission refuses a cell.
nightly.ciJobTimeoutMs.rationale: Pipeline 73185690 (2026-10-12) measured the DocsFab arm. Setup before the first cell took about 31 minutes, and its 13 executed cells took 8244 seconds including J1, a mean of 634 seconds, or 743 seconds excluding two early failures. Its 230-minute script admitted only 13 of the 20 cells. At 743 seconds per cell the twentieth cell starts after about 31 + 19*12.4 = 266 minutes, and its full 60-minute agent-plus-J1 admission plus the five-minute seal reserve run to about 331 minutes. Following the owner's standing direction of generous time budgets with about 2x headroom, the script gets 470 minutes, which still admits the twentieth cell when cells run up to 58 percent slower than measured (the exact limit is 58.96 percent). The 8-hour job leaves ten further minutes for after_script and artifact upload. The dedicated runners' maximum job timeout was raised to 28800 seconds on 2026-10-12. Job and script time are CI bounds outside the comparison series; time admission still labels any unstarted slot arm-time-exhausted.

nightly.ciScriptTimeoutMs.remediation: Stop admitting cells when the remaining script window cannot fit a complete cell and seal reserve; let after_script upload the retained partial artifacts.
nightly.ciScriptTimeoutMs.rationale: The paid arm script gets 470 minutes of the 8-hour GitLab job timeout, leaving ten minutes for artifact handoff. Pipeline 73185690 measured about 31 minutes of setup and 743 seconds per full DocsFab cell including J1, so the twentieth cell starts after about 266 minutes. Its full 60-minute agent-plus-J1 admission and the five-minute seal reserve then fit with 139 minutes to spare, so cells may run up to 58 percent slower than measured. This follows the owner's standing direction of generous time budgets with about 2x headroom. The judge's retries and repair turns reuse the same budgeted judge boundary and so share the judge call's deadline. The skills-agent and basic-agent paces were not yet measured when it was set.

nightly.ciSealReserveMs.remediation: Keep five minutes before the script timeout for the final ledger settlement, checkpoint readback and safe artifact handoff; change only after an executing runner measurement.
nightly.ciSealReserveMs.rationale: A cell is admitted only if its declared agent and judge deadlines fit before this reserve. Five minutes is the controller's final settlement window within the 230-minute script envelope, while ten further minutes remain before GitLab's job timeout for artifact upload.

nightly.ciHeartbeatMs.remediation: Keep a safe controller heartbeat while a paid arm runs; GitLab drops a job that produces no output for an hour.
nightly.ciHeartbeatMs.rationale: One complete agent-plus-judge cell may occupy the declared 60-minute maximum without other stdout. A fixed five-minute static heartbeat prevents GitLab's 60-minute inactivity drop without exposing participant text, environment or provider details.

nightly.ciArmAutomaticRetries.remediation: Keep automatic GitLab retries disabled for paid arm jobs. Inspect the retained arm checkpoint and job-local ledger, then start a new pipeline; a replay inside one pipeline needs independently qualified cross-job accounting.
nightly.ciArmAutomaticRetries.rationale: GitLab's inherited default retries a runner-system or timeout failure once. A paid arm has a job-local gateway ledger, so automatic job replay could recreate a fresh ledger after prior requests or unknown reservations. A replayed arm of a scheduled run would get a second share of the run cap, so zero automatic retries keeps the run within its cap and the arm's partial artifact truthful.

nightly.gateReadyPollIntervalMs.remediation: Keep the gate's fixed marker-check cadence; the existing sandbox seam timeout owns the authorization wait, and a cadence change requires a measured Linux qualification.
nightly.gateReadyPollIntervalMs.rationale: A bind-mounted marker can arrive without a reliable cross-container filesystem watch notification. Four checks per second let the participant see trusted registration promptly without busy-spinning. This is a planning cadence, not a second timeout or spend bound; the Phase 0 Linux qualification must prove the complete path.

nightly.pipelinePageSize.remediation: Keep GitLab pipeline discovery at its documented 100-item REST page maximum; review the API contract before changing this value.
nightly.pipelinePageSize.rationale: GitLab's pipelines listing has a maximum page size of 100. The selector follows every returned page until it finds a successful main push ancestor or exhausts the listing; it never treats a partial page scan as proof that no green build exists.

dashboard.maxCodeChars.remediation: Read the field path the exporter names; a stop code, class, layer, or route is one kebab-case token, so a longer value is prose, not a code, and stays withheld. If a real product code is legitimately longer, raise dashboard.maxCodeChars in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.maxCodeChars.rationale: Longest stop code, failure class, failure layer, or route that the benchmark dashboard's campaign export publishes from a DocsFab Bench report, and that the dashboard accepts from a snapshot. A longer value is withheld and named by its field path. Measured basis, the 654 distinct kebab-case code tokens in packages/runtime/src on 2026-10-05 had a median of 34 characters, a 95th percentile of 51, and a longest of 65 (a limit refusal code); 96 keeps every one with room for longer refusal codes while a pasted sentence still exceeds it.

dashboard.maxModelIdChars.remediation: Read the field path the exporter names; a model id is a short provider and model name, so a longer value is a pasted path, URL, or credential and stays withheld. If a real model id is legitimately longer, raise dashboard.maxModelIdChars in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.maxModelIdChars.rationale: Longest model id that the benchmark dashboard's campaign export publishes from a DocsFab Bench report, and that the dashboard accepts from a snapshot. A longer value is withheld and named by its field path. Measured basis, the model ids in the repository's model profiles and retained benchmark reports on 2026-10-05 had a median of 33 characters and a longest of 40 (nvidia/llama-3.3-nemotron-super-49b-v1.5); 96 leaves room for longer published model names while a pasted URL path or token still exceeds it.

dashboard.maxModelIdSegments.remediation: Read the field path the exporter names; a model id with more slash-separated segments looks like a path or a URL and stays withheld. If a real model id legitimately has more, raise dashboard.maxModelIdSegments in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.maxModelIdSegments.rationale: Most slash-separated segments in a model id that the benchmark dashboard's campaign export publishes, and that the dashboard accepts from a snapshot. A model id with more is withheld and named by its field path. Measured basis, every model id in the repository's model profiles and retained benchmark reports on 2026-10-05 had one to three segments (model, provider/model, or route/provider/model); four leaves one level of headroom while a file path or URL path is refused.

dashboard.maxPhraseChars.remediation: Read the field path the exporter names; a product entry point or stage is a short phrase, so a longer value is prose and stays withheld. If a real entry point or stage is legitimately longer, raise dashboard.maxPhraseChars in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.maxPhraseChars.rationale: Longest product entry point or stage that the benchmark dashboard's campaign export publishes from a DocsFab Bench report, and that the dashboard accepts from a snapshot. A longer value is withheld and named by its field path. Measured basis, the stage names in packages/runtime/src on 2026-10-05 were at most 11 characters, and an entry point is a command such as docsfab run update-documentation (32 characters) with at most a short note; 128 keeps a command with a note while a pasted paragraph exceeds it.

dashboard.history.maxPeriods.remediation: Read which metric the dashboard names; a series longer than this was not written weekly or was never pruned. If the page should keep more history, raise dashboard.history.maxPeriods in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.history.maxPeriods.rationale: Most periods of history the dashboard keeps for one metric and reads back for its trend. 104 is two years of weekly periods, long enough to show a seasonal change and short enough that a series written daily by mistake is refused instead of read. Provisional planning value, not measured; the first quarter of real history.jsonl rows on the pilot host is the basis to revisit it.

dashboard.history.maxBytes.remediation: Inspect history.jsonl for a repeated or runaway writer. If the history legitimately grew past it, raise dashboard.history.maxBytes in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.history.maxBytes.rationale: Largest history.jsonl the dashboard reads. Sizing arithmetic, 8 vital signs x 104 weekly periods is 832 rows, and a nightly series and a per-build series over the same horizon add about 728 rows each at one row a day, so about 2,300 rows; at about 400 bytes a row that is about 0.9 MB, under 1 MiB. 8 MiB leaves about 8 times the headroom while a pasted log or a binary stays out of the parser. Provisional planning value; the first quarter of real history.jsonl size is the basis to revisit it.

dashboard.trend.minPeriodCount.remediation: Read the metric the page names as not enough history; wait for more runs in the period, or widen the period. If a smaller denominator is a fair basis, lower dashboard.trend.minPeriodCount in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.trend.minPeriodCount.rationale: Smallest denominator in either period for a rate change to be called better or worse. Below it the page says there is not enough history instead of naming a direction. With ten runs in a period one failure moves a rate by at most ten points; the significance of the comparison itself comes from localWorkflows.canaryAlertMaxPValue. Provisional planning value, not measured; the spread of weekly denominators across the first real quarter is the basis to revisit it.

dashboard.trend.minEffectPoints.remediation: Review the measured rate and its impact, then change dashboard.trend.minEffectPoints in config/limits/dashboard.yaml if a different minimum matters to operators.
dashboard.trend.minEffectPoints.rationale: A statistical result also needs a five percentage point effect before the dashboard colors it. Pilot jobs are correlated during outages, so high volume alone must not color a tiny shift. Provisional planning value pending a quarter of observed weekly rates.

dashboard.history.settleHours.remediation: Inspect late source delivery, then change dashboard.history.settleHours in config/limits/dashboard.yaml if a different closing delay is justified.
dashboard.history.settleHours.rationale: One day after an ISO week ends lets nightly and exported source records arrive before a week freezes. Later arrivals remain visible as revisions. Provisional planning value pending measured source delivery delay.

dashboard.attention.maxItems.remediation: Change dashboard.attention.maxItems in config/limits/dashboard.yaml if the front page can show a different number while retaining the full ranked list.
dashboard.attention.maxItems.rationale: Six attention items fit the one-screen front page while additional items remain behind its expansion control. Provisional planning value pending the rendered page at 1440 by 900.

dashboard.page.trendPeriods.remediation: Change dashboard.page.trendPeriods in config/limits/dashboard.yaml if operators need a different visible span without changing retained history.
dashboard.page.trendPeriods.rationale: Twelve points show roughly a quarter of weekly direction within a compact vital row. Retained history remains longer. Provisional planning value pending front-page layout evidence.

dashboard.attention.minStreak.remediation: Read the attention list for the streak and its first failing night or build. If a shorter or longer streak should reach the list, change dashboard.attention.minStreak in config/limits/dashboard.yaml.
dashboard.attention.minStreak.rationale: Consecutive failing nights or builds that put a streak on the attention list. Three is the smallest streak that is not a single flake and not a pair coinciding with one bad merge. Provisional planning value, not measured; the false-alarm count on the attention list over the first month is the basis to revisit it.

dashboard.ci.historyWeeks.remediation: Lower dashboard.ci.historyWeeks if the fetch reaches dashboard.ci.maxPages; raise it in config/limits/dashboard.yaml for a longer CI history, and raise dashboard.ci.maxPages with it.
dashboard.ci.historyWeeks.rationale: Weeks of main and nightly pipelines that the dashboard's CI fetch reads back, so a CI trend has a quarter of builds to compare. Twelve weeks is one quarter; the history file, not this fetch, keeps anything older. Provisional planning value, not measured; the weekly span the CI trend needs once real history exists is the basis to revisit it.

dashboard.ci.maxPages.remediation: Read which listing the fetch names. Lower dashboard.ci.historyWeeks, or raise dashboard.ci.maxPages in config/limits/dashboard.yaml; the fetch never keeps a partial listing.
dashboard.ci.maxPages.rationale: Most API pages the dashboard's CI fetch reads for one pipeline listing before it refuses. Sizing arithmetic, about 30 main pipelines in 13 hours on 2026-10-07 is roughly 400 a week, so 12 weeks is about 4,800 pipelines; at 100 per page (the fetch page size) that is 48 pages. 100 pages leaves a little more than twice that for faster merging while a runaway listing is refused. Provisional planning value; the pipeline rate after the first quarter is the basis to revisit it.

dashboard.ci.fetchConcurrency.remediation: If the hourly refresh nears its unit time limit in the CI fetch, raise dashboard.ci.fetchConcurrency in config/limits/dashboard.yaml; if GitLab answers with rate limits, lower it. The fetch log names how many pipelines it fetched and how many it reused.
dashboard.ci.fetchConcurrency.rationale: Most GitLab requests the dashboard's CI fetch keeps in flight at once for per-pipeline reads (a main pipeline's test report summary, a schedule pipeline's jobs). On 2026-10-16 main saw 80 to 100 merges a day, about 2,100 main pipelines in the 12-week window, and each request took 2.3 to 3.9 seconds, so a full fetch one request at a time ran past the refresh unit's 50 minutes. Measured from a Mac the same day with four in flight, a full fetch of 2,110 main pipelines made 2,182 requests in 26.7 minutes, and an incremental fetch that reused all but 3 to 8 of them made 75 to 80 requests in 2.8 to 5.3 minutes. Four is a modest load on GitLab for one read-only client. Value chosen with the fix of 2026-10-16, not measured against GitLab's rate limits.

dashboard.ci.fetchAttempts.remediation: If the refresh fails with refresh-ci-fetch and fetch-ci.mjs, run by hand as the service account, logs a failure that usually passes (HTTP 429 or 5xx, or a connection error before GitLab answered) on its last attempt at a read, raise dashboard.ci.fetchAttempts or dashboard.ci.retryBackoffSeconds in config/limits/dashboard.yaml; for HTTP 429 lower dashboard.ci.fetchConcurrency first. An error that every attempt gets is a GitLab or network fault to report, not a limit to raise.
dashboard.ci.fetchAttempts.rationale: How many times in all the dashboard's CI fetch asks GitLab for one document after a failure that usually passes, which is GitLab answering HTTP 429 or 5xx, or a connection error before any answer. On 2026-10-16 GitLab answered one test_report_summary read of a full fetch with HTTP 500, which failed the whole fetch, and the same read succeeded three times when asked again; a full fetch made 2,182 reads that day, so one brief error can stop it. Three attempts ride out a brief error without hiding a lasting one; any other failure is not asked again. Value chosen with the fix of 2026-10-16, not measured against GitLab's error rate.

dashboard.ci.retryBackoffSeconds.remediation: If reads that the CI fetch asks again still fail with HTTP 429 or connection errors, raise dashboard.ci.retryBackoffSeconds in config/limits/dashboard.yaml so the fetch waits longer before asking again; lower it if the waits make the refresh too slow.
dashboard.ci.retryBackoffSeconds.rationale: How long the dashboard's CI fetch waits before asking GitLab again after a failure that usually passes, doubling before each later attempt, so with three attempts in all a read waits 2 seconds and then 4. A brief server error or a dropped connection usually passes within seconds, and the wait keeps the fetch from asking again at once while GitLab is struggling. Value chosen with the fix of 2026-10-16, not measured; a GitLab rate limit that lasts a minute needs a longer wait or a lower dashboard.ci.fetchConcurrency.

dashboard.ci.reuseSettleMinutes.remediation: If a finished pipeline's test totals on the dashboard differ from GitLab's, raise dashboard.ci.reuseSettleMinutes in config/limits/dashboard.yaml so the fetch reads each finished pipeline again later; lower it only if every hourly fetch rereads too many.
dashboard.ci.reuseSettleMinutes.rationale: How long after a main pipeline's last update the previous CI snapshot must have been taken before the fetch reuses that pipeline's test totals instead of asking GitLab again.
